hints: Use double-angle identities to rewrite the numerator and denominator as squares of single-angle functions.
Cancel the common factor and identify the quotient as $\tan^2\theta$.
walkthrough:
Recall the double-angle formulas for cosine in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$:
$$\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta \implies 1 - \cos 2\theta = 2\sin^2\theta$$
$$\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1 \implies 1 + \cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta$$

Substitute these identities directly into the numerator and denominator of the left-hand side:
$$\dfrac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{1 + \cos 2\theta} = \dfrac{2\sin^2\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}$$

Cancel the factor of $2$ and simplify using $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$:
$$\dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} = \left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 = \tan^2\theta$$
Therefore:
$$\dfrac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{1 + \cos 2\theta} \equiv \tan^2\theta$$
This completes the proof.

hints: Use the identity from part (a), then integrate $\tan^2\theta$ by rewriting it with $\sec^2\theta$.
Evaluate at $\pi/3$ and $\pi/6$, using exact tangent values and simplifying the radical difference.
walkthrough:
Replace the integrand using the identity proved in part (a):
$$\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{1 + \cos 2\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \tan^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Use the Pythagorean identity $\tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta - 1$ to rewrite the integrand:
$$\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} (\sec^2\theta - 1)\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Integrate term by term, using $\int \sec^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \tan\theta$ and $\int 1\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \theta$:
$$\left[\tan\theta - \theta\right]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\left(\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \left(\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

Simplify the coefficients:
$$\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$$
$$\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{2\pi - \pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$
Thus the exact value is:
$$\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} \quad \left(\text{or } \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$
